findings.title: Multiple-provider guard removed; equal-order providers are now picked silently by classpath order
findings.body:
`detectProvider` used to throw `IllegalStateException` when more than one `CryptoProvider` was found. That check protected against a misconfigured classpath, for example one containing both `keycloak-crypto-default` and `keycloak-crypto-fips1402`.

Now the list is sorted by `order()` and the first entry is used. `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider` and `FIPS1402Provider` all return 200, and the sort is stable, so a tie between them is broken by ServiceLoader/classpath order. The other providers are reported only at DEBUG level.

Consequences:
- A FIPS deployment that accidentally has the default provider on the classpath can silently run with the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider instead of failing fast.
- `ServiceLoader` instantiates every provider before sorting. The ignored providers' constructors still run their global side effects: FIPS inserts BCFIPS/BCJSSE at JVM security-provider positions 1-3 and rewrites `ssl.*ManagerFactory.algorithm`, and Default registers BC. The JVM can end up in a mixed state.

Suggested fix: keep failing (or at least log at WARN) when two or more providers share the highest order. Only allow silent fallback when the winner has a strictly higher order, such as 200 vs the authz-client's 100.

findings.title: New abstract interface method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body:
`int order();` is added to the public `CryptoProvider` interface in keycloak-common without a default implementation. Any `CryptoProvider` implemented outside this repository stops compiling, or fails at runtime with `AbstractMethodError` when `CryptoIntegration` calls `order()` while sorting. This includes custom providers and implementations in keycloak-client or other downstream projects built against a newer keycloak-common.

A `default int order() { return 0; }` (or similar) would keep compatibility and still let the bundled providers override it.

findings.title: ES384/ES512 tests use a P-256 key, so real curve sizes and long-form DER lengths are never tested
findings.body:
The key pair comes from `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()`, which defaults to P-256. The same 32-byte r/s values are reused for ES384 and ES512; they are only zero-padded to 48/66 bytes.

As a result:
- P-384 and P-521 signatures are never exercised.
- A P-521 DER signature is about 139 bytes. That is the only case that triggers the long-form length (>127) path in `ASN1Encoder.writeLength` and `ASN1Decoder.readLength`, and it stays untested.

The test also only checks that the custom encoder and decoder agree with each other. It never compares `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` output with the JDK-produced DER (`sign`), and never checks that the result passes `Signature.verify`. Symmetric bugs in the hand-written ASN.1 code would therefore go unnoticed.

Suggested fix: initialize the generator with `secp256r1`/`secp384r1`/`secp521r1` per algorithm, and assert `Arrays.equals(asn1Des, sign)` or verify the re-encoded signature.

findings.title: Leftover encoder calls whose results are discarded
findings.body:
`ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` (lines 114-115) build encoders and throw them away. They are re-created inside the `writeDerSeq` call just below.

This is dead code that does extra allocation and encoding on every signature verification, and it makes readers wonder whether something was meant to use those results. Remove both lines.
